passage: The clay pot fell out of Sharmila's hands as she rushed across the classroom in the crowded corridor, and it cracked on the floor. It was Minakshi's pot, made for the school display and due to be shown in ten minutes. Sharmila's heart thumped. She wanted to say “It just slipped” but she did not. “I broke it,” she said. “I'm sorry. I was running.” Minakshi's eyes filled. Sharmila added, “I can help you fix it with glue, or make another with you at lunch.” Minakshi took a breath. “Let's glue it first.” They found the teacher, and together they mended the pot.

qa.q: Whose pot broke?
qa.a: Minakshi's.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling when she said “I broke it”?
qa.a: She felt guilty and worried, since her heart thumped, and she chose to own up instead of making an excuse.

qa.q: What made Sharmila's apology repair more than a vague sorry?
qa.a: She named exactly what she did, said she was running and offered to fix or remake the pot.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt at first, and what changed?
qa.a: She was upset and near tears at first, then more settled when Sharmila offered specific help. 🤍

grounding: A child says I broke it, I'm sorry, and offers to help fix it, naming the act and offering a remedy.

passage: “I broke your torch, Jagdish,” said Afreen at the door, holding the two pieces. “I was using it under the bed and it fell. I'm really sorry.” Jagdish looked at it, then at her. “It was my birthday present.” Afreen swallowed. “I know. I'll give you my pocket money for a new one, or we can take it to the repair shop together this weekend. Which do you want?” Jagdish sighed. “Repair shop, I think.” Afreen's shoulders dropped. She said, “Thank you for letting me help.” Jagdish put a hand on the pieces. “Thanks for telling me the truth.”

qa.q: What did Afreen break?
qa.a: Jagdish's torch.

qa.q: What was Jagdish probably feeling when saying it was a birthday present?
qa.a: Jagdish was probably hurt and sad about losing something special, though also willing to accept help.

qa.q: Why is Afreen's apology more repairing than a vague sorry?
qa.a: She named what she did, said she was sorry and offered a real remedy with a choice.

qa.q: How might Afreen have felt while she waited for Jagdish's answer?
qa.a: She probably felt anxious and guilty, and relieved when Jagdish chose the repair shop.

grounding: A child says I broke it, I'm sorry, and offers to replace or fix it, naming the act and the remedy.

passage: “Irawati. I have to tell you something.” Shalini held out her hands. In them were the two halves of Irawati's clay elephant. “I knocked it off the shelf with my bag. It was my fault. I'm really sorry.” Irawati stared at the pieces. “I worked on that for a week.” “I know. I can see the trunk took ages.” Shalini swallowed. “Can I help you fix it? My brother has proper clay glue. Or I'll help you make a new one at break, for as long as it takes.” Irawati was quiet. Then she took one half. “The glue. And you hold the trunk while it dries.” “Deal.”

qa.q: What did Shalini break?
qa.a: Shalini broke Irawati's clay elephant.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling when she stared at the pieces?
qa.a: Irawati felt upset and disappointed, having worked on the elephant for a week.

qa.q: What made Shalini's apology repairing?
qa.a: She named exactly what she did, took the blame and offered a real fix: glue, or help making a new one.

qa.q: What would change if Shalini had just said “Sorry if you're upset”?
qa.a: Irawati might have felt the apology was empty, and the elephant would have stayed broken.

grounding: Shows a child naming the specific act, saying sorry and offering to help fix what she broke.

passage: I'm Nitin. Last year I borrowed my neighbour Yogesh's comic, the one his uncle brought from Kolkata, and I left it on the bus. I didn't tell him for a week. Every time he asked, I said, “I'll bring it tomorrow.” My stomach hurt every tomorrow. Finally, I went to his door. “I lost your comic on the bus. It's my fault. I should've told you on the first day.” Yogesh's face went red. “My uncle gave me that.” “I know. I asked at the bus depot; it's not there. I've saved my pocket money for a new copy, and Papa says he'll take us to the bookshop on Sunday.” Yogesh was cross for two days. On Sunday, he came.

qa.q: Where did Nitin leave the comic?
qa.a: Nitin left the comic on the bus.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling during the week of saying “tomorrow”?
qa.a: Nitin felt guilty and anxious, with a stomach ache every time Yogesh asked.

qa.q: What made Nitin's apology more repairing than a vague sorry?
qa.a: Nitin named exactly what happened, admitted the delay, checked the depot and offered a replacement with a plan to buy it.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel about losing the comic?
qa.a: Yogesh was upset and cross for two days, since his uncle had given it to him, but he came on Sunday.

grounding: Shows a child admitting a specific fault and offering to replace what was lost, which repairs more than a vague sorry.

passage: Class note, Wednesday. Hansa, Class 5. At lunch today a cricket ball went through the staff-room window. By the time I got outside, the boys had scattered, except Tarun. He walked straight up to me, white-faced, and said, “Ma'am, I hit it. It was my shot. I'm sorry.” Not “it was an accident”, not “sorry if anyone's cross”, just what he did. Then he asked, “Can I help clean up the glass, or help fix it?” I didn't let him touch the glass, but I let him hold the tools for the handyman after school. He watched the new pane go in. I've written to his parents that he told the truth first.

qa.q: What did Tarun hold after school?
qa.a: Tarun held the tools for the handyman.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling when he walked up to Hansa?
qa.a: Tarun felt scared and guilty, white-faced, but determined to own up.

qa.q: How did Hansa respond to Tarun's admission, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She kept him away from the glass but let him help the handyman, and told his parents he told the truth first, rewarding honesty.

qa.q: What might the other boys have felt when they scattered?
qa.a: They were probably scared of getting into trouble, unlike Tarun, who stayed and owned up.

grounding: Shows a child admitting a specific fault and offering to help fix it, and an adult rewarding the honesty safely.

passage:
Tuesday

I have to write this because I feel bad. In art I bumped Vinita's clay elephant off the shelf, and its trunk snapped. First I said, "Sorry if you're upset," and walked off, which was rubbish. Vinita didn't talk to me all through lunch. At home, Mum asked what I was actually sorry for.

Today before the bell, I went up to Vinita and said, "I knocked your elephant off and broke the trunk. I'm sorry. Can I stay after school and help you fix it, or make a new trunk with you?" Vinita looked at me for a long time, then said, "You do the glue. I'll do the shape." It looks a bit wonky now, but she smiled.

Elizabeth

qa.q: What part of Vinita's clay elephant snapped?
qa.a: Its trunk.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel after the first "Sorry if you're upset"?
qa.a: Guilty and uncomfortable, calling it rubbish, especially when Vinita stayed silent all through lunch.

qa.q: What made the second apology better?
qa.a: Elizabeth named the specific act, "I knocked your elephant off and broke the trunk", said sorry and offered to help fix it.

qa.q: How did Vinita likely feel about the two apologies?
qa.a: The vague one probably felt careless and left her hurt; the specific one with an offer of help made her willing to fix it together and smile.

grounding: It is a child's diary contrasting a vague sorry with an apology that names the act and offers to help repair it.
